docs.title: Polynx
docs.text: String-powered Polars expression engine with extended DataFrame and LazyFrame utilities.

docs.title: What is Polynx?
docs.text:
Polynx bridges the gap between the intuitive, concise expression syntax of Pandas/SQL and the ultra-fast execution engine of Polars.

With Polynx, you can write filtering criteria, multi-statement mutations, conditional branching (case_when, select, where), and group aggregations using simple string expressions without verbose nested method calls—all while retaining the speed, thread safety, and query planning of Polars.

Relationship to Polars

Polynx is built on top of Polars. It wraps native Polars objects while inheriting all built-in methods.

This documentation focuses exclusively on Polynx-specific extensions. For native Polars functions, methods, expressions, and algorithms, refer directly to the Official Polars Python API Reference.

docs.title: Key Highlights
docs.text:
• String-Powered Queries: Query DataFrames with Pandas-like syntax: df.query("@min_val <= A < @max_val & B in @cats").
  • Conditional Branching (case_when): Cleanly handle multi-branch logic (case_when([cond1, cond2], [res1, res2], default)) without nested .when().then().otherwise() structures.
  • Multi-Statement Assignments (wc): Mutate and create multiple columns in a single call with semicolon-separated assignments: df.wc("A_sum = A.sum().over('B'); E_mean = E.mean()").
  • First-Class LazyFrames: Every string operation, aggregation, and filter runs seamlessly in both eager DataFrame and lazy LazyFrame contexts.
  • Extended DataFrame Utilities: Shorthand helpers for deduplication (dd), sorting (dsort/asort), pivoting (unstack), counting (vcnt/ucnt), and summary statistics (describe(group_keys=...)).
  • High-Performance Caching: Built-in LRU and hash expression caching with automatic cache-bypassing when dynamic loop variables are detected.
  • 100% Polars Interoperability: Transparent wrappers around Polars types; all Polars functions and methods are inherited and available out of the box.

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
import polynx as plx

# Create a DataFrame
df = plx.DataFrame({
    'A': [1, 2, 3, 4],
    'B': ['abc', 'bc', 'aaa', None],
    'C': ['2023-01-01', '2021-01-01', '2009-11-01', '2000-11-11'],
    'E': [1.1, 2.1, 3.5, 0.0]
}).wc("C = C.str.to_date('%Y-%m-%d')")

# Filter rows using string expressions with variable substitution
threshold = 2
result = df.query("A >= @threshold & B.str.contains('a|b')")

# Add conditional logic and multi-statement assignments
enhanced = result.wc(
    "Tier = case_when([A < 3, B in ['bc']], ['Bronze', 'Silver'], 'Gold');"
    "Score = A * 10 + E"
)

docs.title: Why not just use Polars directly?
docs.text: You can, and polynx doesn't replace it. Native Polars is a good choice when your expressions are fixed in code. polynx is shorter for quick filters and column math, and it lets an expression live in a string (a config, a notebook cell, generated code). You can mix both in the same pipeline.

docs.title: How much overhead does polynx add?
docs.text: For a repeated query, essentially none: the string becomes a native Polars expression and Polars does the work. A string seen for the first time costs about 0.1 ms to parse; after that it is cached, and loops with changing values (A > 1, A > 2, ...) reuse a parsed template. See the benchmark and run benchmarks/bench.py to measure on your own data.

docs.title: How is it different from pl.sql_expr / SQLContext?
docs.text: Polars' SQL support parses faster (it is written in Rust, roughly 30 µs per expression against polynx's ~100 µs), but it uses SQL syntax. polynx follows pandas/Python syntax: @var variables, method chaining such as A.mean().over('B'), backticked column names, case_when, and user-defined functions.

docs.title: Does it use eval()? Is it safe?
docs.text: Expression text is parsed by a grammar and is never passed to Python's eval(). The functions a string can call are limited to a small set of builtins, functions you register with register_udf, and names in the calling scope. It is not a sandbox: @name and bare function names resolve against the caller's scope, so a string can use anything the calling code can see. Don't evaluate strings from untrusted users where sensitive objects are in scope.

docs.title: Does it work with LazyFrame?
docs.text: Yes. Every string method works on eager and lazy frames, and Polars' optimizer still sees the whole query.

docs.title: Do I have to wrap my DataFrames?
docs.text: No. Besides the wrapper classes (plx.DataFrame, plx.LazyFrame), importing polynx registers a .plx namespace on native Polars objects: pl_df.plx.query("A > 2").

docs.title: Which Python and Polars versions are supported?
docs.text: CI runs on Python 3.9 to 3.13, and also against the minimum supported Polars (1.8) as well as the latest release.

docs.title: I found a bug or want new syntax. Where do I go?
docs.text: Questions and syntax ideas belong in Discussions. Bugs with a reproducible example go in Issues; please include your polynx and Polars versions.

docs.title: Via PyPI (Recommended)
docs.text:
Install Polynx via pip:

pip install polynx

docs.title: From Source
docs.text:
Clone the GitHub repository and install it in editable mode:

git clone https://github.com/LowellWinston/polynx.git
cd polynx
pip install -e .

docs.title: Core Concept: Drop-in Polars Wrapper
docs.text:
Polynx wraps Polars' DataFrame, LazyFrame, Series, and Expr. Any operation valid in Polars is valid in Polynx:

import polynx as plx
import polars as pl

# Create a Polynx DataFrame
df = plx.DataFrame({
    'category': ['X', 'X', 'Y', 'Y'],
    'val1': [10, 20, 30, 40],
    'val2': [1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5]
})

# Access native Polars methods directly
print(df.shape)
print(df.columns)
print(df.schema)

# Access all top-level Polars functions directly via plx
df2 = plx.concat([df, df])

docs.title: Conversions
docs.text:
You can convert between Polynx and native Polars or Pandas DataFrames at any time:

# Convert to native Polars
native_polars_df = df.to_polars()
assert isinstance(native_polars_df, pl.DataFrame)

# Convert to Pandas
pandas_df = df.to_pandas()

docs.title: Your First Polynx Workflow
docs.text:
Here is a typical workflow demonstrating how Polynx streamlines common data analysis steps:

import polynx as plx

# 1. Initialize data
df = plx.DataFrame({
    'user_id': [101, 102, 103, 104],
    'tier': ['silver', 'gold', 'bronze', 'silver'],
    'spend': [150.0, 450.0, 50.0, 220.0],
    'active': [True, True, False, True]
})

# 2. Filter using query with variable substitution
target_spend = 100.0
active_customers = df.query("spend >= @target_spend & active == True")

# 3. Add calculated columns using wc (with_columns)
enriched = active_customers.wc(
    "discount = case_when(spend > 300, 0.20, 0.10);"
    "net_spend = spend * (1 - discount);"
    "mean_tier_spend = spend.mean().over('tier')"
)

# 4. Aggregate with group-by and subtotal
summary = enriched.gb('tier', 'spend.sum(); net_spend.sum()', with_subtotal=True)
print(summary)

Proceed to the Expression Engine Guide for full syntax details.

docs.title: Caching & Performance
docs.text:
Parsing string expressions involves generating an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) through Lark. For applications running repetitive transformations or building pipelines across thousands of partitions, repeated parsing can introduce unnecessary latency.

Polynx includes an internal expression caching subsystem to eliminate parsing overhead.

docs.title: Cache Modes
docs.text:
Polynx provides four caching backends:

Mode Description Best For "raw" (default) Standard dictionary keyed by raw query string Typical analytical scripts "hash" Dictionary keyed by SHA1 hash of query string Long or complex queries "custom_lru" Fixed-size LRU cache Memory-constrained or long-running servers "none" Disables caching completely Debugging or testing

docs.title: Configuring the Cache
docs.text:
import polynx as plx

# Set caching mode
plx.config.set_cache_mode("custom_lru")

# Configure capacity (for custom_lru)
plx.config.set_cache_max_size(2000)

# Check active settings
mode = plx.config.get_cache_mode()
max_size = plx.config.get_cache_max_size()

docs.title: @var and Changing Values
docs.text:
When an expression contains variable substitution syntax (@var), Polynx skips the exact-string result cache, so a changed variable is never served stale:

for i in [1, 2, 3]:
    df.query("A == @i")   # @i is re-read on every call

Polynx also keeps a template cache: literals (numbers and quoted strings) are stripped from the expression, the parse tree for that shape is compiled once, and only the literal values are bound per call. Loops such as A > 1, A > 2, ... and @var queries therefore avoid re-parsing even though no two strings are identical. Setting the cache mode to "none" disables it.

docs.title: Cache Diagnostics & Maintenance
docs.text:
Inspect cache state and clear memory when necessary:

import polynx as plx

# Inspect cache items
cache_contents = plx.expr_parser.get_expr_cache()

# Inspect size
current_size = plx.expr_parser.get_expr_cache_size()

# Inspect hit/miss statistics
stats = plx.expr_parser.get_expr_cache_stats()
print(f"Hits: {stats['hit']}, Misses: {stats['miss']}")

# Reset cache and metrics
plx.clear_all_expr_caches()
plx.expr_parser.reset_expr_cache_stats()

docs.title: Extended DataFrame Utilities
docs.text: Polynx patches both DataFrame and LazyFrame with common productivity utilities inspired by Pandas and SQL.

docs.title: Deduplication: dd()
docs.text:
Deduplicates rows while maintaining row order and keeping the first occurrence:

import polynx as plx

df = plx.DataFrame({'A': [1, 1, 2, 3], 'B': ['x', 'x', 'y', 'z']})
df.dd()

(Equivalent to df.unique(maintain_order=True, keep='first'))

docs.title: Sorting: dsort() and asort()
docs.text:
Quick descending and ascending sorting:

# Sort descending by specific column(s)
df.dsort('A')

# If 'by' is omitted, sorts by all columns
df.dsort()

# Sort ascending
df.asort('A')

docs.title: Pivoting: unstack()
docs.text:
Pivots a DataFrame using the last two columns as the pivot key and value columns, sorted by index:

df_long = plx.DataFrame({
    'user_id': [1, 1, 2, 2],
    'metric': ['score', 'level', 'score', 'level'],
    'val': [95, 3, 80, 2]
})

df_long.unstack()

docs.title: Frequency Counts with vcnt(col=None)
docs.text:
Computes frequency counts of values in specified column(s), sorted in descending order:

# Value count on column 'B'
df.vcnt('B')

# If omitted, computes frequency across all columns
df.vcnt()

docs.title: Unique Count with ucnt(col=None)
docs.text:
Returns the total number of distinct rows/values as an integer scalar:

distinct_count = df.ucnt('A')

docs.title: String GroupBy: gb()
docs.text:
Aggregate grouped data with string expressions.

# Group by 'B' and calculate sum of A and mean of E
df.gb('B', "A.sum(); E.mean()")

docs.title: Automatic Subtotals & Total Row
docs.text:
Enable with_subtotal=True to compute hierarchical subtotals and an 'All' summary row:

df.gb('B', "A.sum()", with_subtotal=True)

For multi-key groupings (df.gb(['Region', 'City'], ...)), with_subtotal=True calculates intermediate totals for each higher level before appending the global summary.

docs.title: Grouped Descriptive Statistics: describe()
docs.text:
Extends Polars' native .describe() by supporting grouping keys:

# Computes count, null_count, mean, std, min, 25%, 50%, 75%, max grouped by 'B'
df.describe(group_keys='B', selected_columns=['A', 'E']).round(2)

docs.title: Float Utilities: round() and cum_max()
docs.text:
• df.round(decimal=2): Rounds all floating-point columns across the DataFrame without having to list them manually.
  • df.cum_max(): Computes cumulative maximum across all floating-point columns.
df.round(2)
df.cum_max()

docs.title: Scalar Extraction & List Conversion
docs.text:
• df.to_list(col_name=None): Extracts column as a Python list (defaults to first column).
  • df.max(col_name=None): Returns scalar maximum value.
  • df.min(col_name=None): Returns scalar minimum value.
a_values = df.to_list('A')  # [1, 2, 3, 4]
max_a = df.max('A')         # 4
min_a = df.min('A')         # 1

docs.title: Rename by List: rename()
docs.text:
In addition to Polars' standard dictionary rename syntax, Polynx allows renaming columns with a list of new names matching the number of columns:

df.rename(['Col_1', 'Col_2', 'Col_3', 'Col_4'])

docs.title: Memory Footprint: size()
docs.text:
Prints the estimated DataFrame memory footprint and optionally returns the size:

# Print to console (DataFrame size: 0.12 MB)
df.size(unit='mb')

# Return numeric size value
size_kb = df.size(unit='kb', return_size=True)

docs.title: Quick Visualization: pplot()
docs.text:
Provides pandas-style .plot() directly from a Polynx DataFrame, setting the first column as index:

df.select(['Date', 'Revenue']).pplot(kind='line')         # plx.DataFrame / plx.LazyFrame
pl_df.select(['Date', 'Revenue']).plx.pplot(kind='line')  # native polars objects

docs.title: Pandas-Style Merge: plx.merge()
docs.text:
Merges two DataFrames or LazyFrames with automatic suffix handling for overlapping column names:

left = plx.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2], 'val': [10, 20]})
right = plx.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2], 'val': [30, 40]})

merged = plx.merge(left, right, on='id', how='inner', suffixes=('_left', '_right'))

docs.title: Window Rolling Product: Expr.rolling_prod()
docs.text:
Polynx patches plx.Expr with a rolling product calculation (numerically computed via log-sum-exp):

df.select(plx.col('A').rolling_prod(window_size=2, min_samples=1))

docs.title: Expression Engine
docs.text: Polynx includes an AST-based string expression parser built on Lark that parses string statements into native Polars expression trees.

docs.title: Row Filtering with query()
docs.text:
The .query() method provides an intuitive, high-level syntax for row filtering:

import polynx as plx

df = plx.DataFrame({
    'A': [1, 2, 3, 4],
    'B': ['abc', 'bc', 'aaa', None],
    'C': ['2023-01-01', '2021-01-01', '2009-11-01', '2000-11-11'],
    'E': [1.1, 2.1, 3.5, 0.0]
}).wc("C = C.str.to_date('%Y-%m-%d')")

docs.title: Chained Comparisons
docs.text:
df.query("1 <= A < 4")
df.query("'2001-01-01' < C < '2022-01-01'")

docs.title: Logical Operators and Negation
docs.text:
Use & (AND), | (OR), ~ (Bitwise NOT), or the keyword not: 

df.query("A > 1 & E < 3.0")
df.query("not (B.is_null() & A.is_not_null())")

docs.title: Set Membership (in and not in)
docs.text:
df.query("B in ['aaa', 'bc']")
df.query("B not in ['abc']")

docs.title: String Operations
docs.text:
df.query("B.str.contains('a|b')")
df.query("B.str.ends_with('c')")
df.query("B.str.starts_with('a')")

docs.title: Arithmetic Filtering
docs.text: df.query("A ** 2 - E > 1")

docs.title: Variable Substitution (@var)
docs.text:
Prefixing a variable with @ dynamically pulls its value from the surrounding Python scope:

low_bound = 1
high_bound = 3
target_categories = ['bc', 'aaa']

df.query("@low_bound <= A < @high_bound & B in @target_categories")

Supported variable types include: - Scalars: numbers, strings, booleans, dates - Sequences: lists, tuples, numpy arrays, pandas Series, polars Series

docs.title: Safety in Loops
docs.text:
Polynx automatically bypasses expression caching whenever @ is detected in the query string, ensuring that loop iterations with changing variables execute accurately:

results = []
for val in [1, 2, 3]:
    sub_df = df.query("A == @val")
    results.append(sub_df)

docs.title: Multi-Statement Assignments with wc()
docs.text:
The .wc() (shorthand for with_columns) method allows sequential column assignments separated by semicolons (;):

df_enriched = df.wc(
    "A_sum = A.sum().over('B');"
    "E_mean = E.mean();"
    "Normalized_E = E / E_mean"
)

You can also mix string expressions and native Polars expressions: 

import polars as pl

df_enriched = df.wc(
    "Flag = A > 2",
    pl.col("E") * 10
)

docs.title: Expression Evaluation: eval() and assign()
docs.text:
• df.eval(expr_str, mode='select'): Evaluates the expression and returns only the calculated column(s).
  • df.assign(expr_str): Evaluates the expression and returns the entire DataFrame with the new columns appended.
# Returns single column DataFrame with result
df.eval("(A ** 2 - E) / (10 - A)")

# Appends new column to DataFrame
df.assign("Result = (A ** 2 - E) / (10 - A)")

docs.title: Conditional Branching
docs.text: Polynx provides built-in conditional logic functions inside string expressions:

docs.title: case_when(conds, choices, default)
docs.text:
A unified conditional function that supports both multi-condition and single-condition branching:

# Multi-condition: pass lists of conditions and choices
df.wc("Tier = case_when([A < 2, B in ['bc']], ['Bronze', 'Silver'], 'Gold')")

# Single-condition: pass single condition and choice
df.wc("High_Flag = case_when(A > 2, 1, 0)")

docs.title: select(conds, choices, default)
docs.text:
Mirrors numpy.select for multi-condition branching:

df.wc("Category = select([A == 1, A == 2], ['First', 'Second'], 'Other')")

docs.title: where(cond, choice, default)
docs.text:
Mirrors numpy.where for ternary branching:

df.wc("Status = where(A >= 3, 'High', 'Low')")

docs.title: Date Arithmetic: mondf()
docs.text:
Calculate the number of elapsed months between two date/datetime columns:

df.wc("month_gap = mondf(C, C.shift())")

Calculated via: (end_date.year - beg_date.year) * 12 + end_date.month - beg_date.month.

docs.title: Horizontal Aggregations
docs.text:
Polars' horizontal aggregations are available in string expressions:

df.wc(
    "row_max = max_horizontal(A, E);"
    "row_min = min_horizontal(A, E)"
)

docs.title: Window Functions with .over()
docs.text:
Compute windowed calculations over one or more grouping keys:

# Single key
df.wc("B_avg = A.mean().over('B')")

# Multiple keys
df.wc("Multi_avg = A.mean().over(['B', 'C'])")

docs.title: Column Names with Spaces (Backticks)
docs.text:
Wrap column identifiers containing spaces, dashes, or special characters in backticks (`):

df_space = plx.DataFrame({"Total Revenue": [100, 200], "Customer ID": [1, 2]})
df_space.query("`Total Revenue` > 150 & `Customer ID` == 2")

docs.title: Custom UDF Registration
docs.text:
Register custom Python functions to invoke them inside string expressions:

import polynx as plx

def square_plus_c(x, c=1):
    return x ** 2 + c

# Register function
plx.register_udf("square_plus_c", square_plus_c)

# Use in string expression
df.wc("Custom_Calc = square_plus_c(A, 5)")

You can also register functions by name from an existing module:

import math
plx.register_udfs_by_names(math, ['sin', 'cos', 'sqrt'])

docs.title: Security Notes
docs.text: Expression text is parsed by a grammar and is never passed to Python's eval(). Functions callable from a string are limited to a small set of pure builtins (abs, round, min, max, sum, len, int, float, str, bool, pow, list, tuple), functions you register with register_udf, and names in the calling scope. @name and bare function names resolve against that calling scope, so a string can use any variable or function the calling code can see. Treat strings from untrusted sources accordingly, and keep sensitive objects out of the scope where you evaluate them.

docs.title: First-Class LazyFrames
docs.text: Polynx treats LazyFrame as a first-class citizen. Every string expression, assignment, and utility method is fully patched onto LazyFrame.

docs.title: Lazy Execution Pipeline
docs.text:
Build entire query pipelines with strings and execute them with .collect():

import polynx as plx

# Initialize eager DataFrame and convert to lazy
df = plx.DataFrame({
    'category': ['A', 'A', 'B', 'B'],
    'val': [10, 20, 30, 40]
})
lazy_df = df.lazy()

# Build pipeline lazily
pipeline = (
    lazy_df
    .wc("val_doubled = val * 2")
    .query("val_doubled > 30")
    .gb("category", "val_doubled.sum()")
)

# Execute query plan
result = pipeline.collect()
print(result)

docs.title: Lazy Indexing Syntax
docs.text:
Polynx enhances LazyFrame with natural indexing syntax:

# Select a single column lazily
lazy_df['val']

# Select multiple columns lazily
lazy_df[['category', 'val']]

# Filter rows using an expression
lazy_df[plx.col('val') > 15]

docs.title: Lazy Conversions
docs.text:
Convert directly to Pandas or Polars:

# .to_pandas() automatically calls .collect() under the hood
pandas_df = lazy_df.to_pandas()

# Retrieve underlying native polars.LazyFrame
native_lazy = lazy_df.to_polars()

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: Welcome to the Polynx API reference. This section contains detailed documentation of all classes, methods, and functions provided by Polynx.

docs.title: Reference Sections

docs.title: Configuration & Cache Reference
docs.text: Polynx provides global configuration settings and cache management tools in polynx.config and polynx.expr_parser.

docs.title: set_cache_mode
docs.text:
Configure the caching backend used by the string expression engine.

plx.config.set_cache_mode(mode: str) -> None

Parameters:

Parameter Type Description mode str Caching mode: "raw", "hash", "custom_lru", or "none".

Modes: - "raw": In-memory dictionary indexed by raw query string. - "hash": SHA1 hashed cache for query strings. - "custom_lru": Fixed-capacity LRU cache. - "none": Disables caching completely.

docs.title: get_cache_mode
docs.text:
Retrieve the current active caching mode.

plx.config.get_cache_mode() -> str

docs.title: set_cache_max_size
docs.text:
Configure maximum cache size for caching backends.

plx.config.set_cache_max_size(size: int) -> None

docs.title: get_cache_max_size
docs.text:
Retrieve current maximum cache size setting.

plx.config.get_cache_max_size() -> int

docs.title: clear_all_expr_caches
docs.text:
Clear all in-memory expression caches across all backends.

plx.clear_all_expr_caches() -> None

docs.text:

plx.expr_parser.get_expr_cache() -> dict

docs.title: get_expr_cache_size

plx.expr_parser.get_expr_cache_size() -> int

plx.expr_parser.get_expr_cache_stats() -> dict[str, int]

plx.expr_parser.reset_expr_cache_stats() -> None

docs.title: DataFrame Reference
docs.text:
polynx.DataFrame is a transparent wrapper around polars.DataFrame that inherits all native Polars methods while adding string expression capabilities and productivity helpers.

import polynx as plx

df = plx.DataFrame(data)

Standard Polars DataFrame Methods

polynx.DataFrame inherits all native Polars methods (e.g. .filter(), .select(), .join(), .group_by(), .pivot(), etc.).

This page documents only the Polynx-specific extension methods. For native Polars DataFrame methods, please refer to the Official Polars DataFrame Reference.

docs.title: query
docs.text:
Filter rows of the DataFrame using an intuitive string expression.

df.query(query_str: str) -> DataFrame

Parameters:

Parameter Type Description query_str str A filter expression string supporting comparison operators, boolean logic (&, |, ~, not), membership (in, not in), string methods, and variable substitution (@var).

Returns: - DataFrame: A filtered DataFrame containing only matching rows.

Examples: 

# Simple comparison
df.query("A > 10")

# Chained comparison with variables
min_val, max_val = 1, 5
df.query("@min_val <= A < @max_val & B in ['x', 'y']")

# Date and string filtering
df.query("Date > '2022-01-01' & Name.str.contains('admin')")

docs.title: eval
docs.text:
Evaluate an expression or mathematical operation string.

df.eval(query_str: str | list[str], mode: str = "select") -> DataFrame

Parameters:

Parameter Type Default Description query_str str or list[str] required The expression string or list of expression strings to evaluate. mode str "select" Evaluation mode. "select" returns only the evaluated columns. "assign" appends the evaluated columns to the DataFrame.

Returns: - DataFrame: Evaluated columns in "select" mode, or the mutated DataFrame in "assign" mode.

Examples: 

# Select mode (returns only the calculated column)
df.eval("(A ** 2 - E) / (10 - A)")

# Multiple expressions
df.eval(["A * 2", "E + 10"])

docs.title: assign
docs.text:
Convenience alias for df.eval(query_str, mode="assign"). Appends evaluated columns to the DataFrame.

df.assign(query_str: str | list[str]) -> DataFrame

Parameters:

Parameter Type Description query_str str or list[str] Assignment string (e.g., "New_Col = A * 10").

Returns: - DataFrame: The DataFrame with new column(s) appended.

Examples: 

df.assign("Total_Score = (A * 10) + E")

docs.title: wc
docs.text:
Extended with_columns supporting multi-statement assignment strings separated by semicolons (;), lists of expressions, and native Polars expressions.

df.wc(*args, **kwargs) -> DataFrame

Parameters:

Parameter Type Description *args str, Expr, or list Expression strings, multi-statement strings, or Polars expressions. **kwargs Expr Standard Polars keyword column assignments.

Returns: - DataFrame: The DataFrame with updated or added columns.

Examples: 

# Multi-statement string assignment
df.wc("A_sum = A.sum().over('B'); E_mean = E.mean(); Ratio = A / E_mean")

# Mixing strings and native Polars expressions
import polars as pl
df.wc("Flag = A > 2", pl.col("E") * 100)

docs.title: gb
docs.text:
String-powered group-by aggregation with optional hierarchical subtotal rows.

df.gb(gp_keys: str | list[str], expr: str, with_subtotal: bool = False) -> DataFrame

Parameters:

Parameter Type Default Description gp_keys str or list[str] required One or more column names to group by. expr str required Semicolon-separated string aggregation expressions (e.g. "A.sum(); E.mean()"). with_subtotal bool False When True, automatically appends hierarchical subtotal rows and an 'All' summary row.

Returns: - DataFrame: Aggregated DataFrame sorted by group keys.

Examples: 

# Basic aggregation
df.gb("Category", "Sales.sum(); Margin.mean()")

# Multi-key with subtotal
df.gb(["Region", "Category"], "Sales.sum()", with_subtotal=True)

docs.title: describe
docs.text:
Extended summary statistics. When group_keys is provided, computes grouped summary metrics (count, null_count, mean, std, min, quantiles, max) across numeric columns.

df.describe(
    group_keys: str | list[str] | None = None,
    selected_columns: list[str] | None = None,
    percentiles: tuple[float, ...] = (0.25, 0.5, 0.75),
    interpolation: str = "nearest"
) -> DataFrame

Parameters:

Parameter Type Default Description group_keys str, list[str], or None None Column(s) to group by for statistics. If None, calls Polars' native .describe(). selected_columns list[str] or None None Numeric columns to summarize. Defaults to all numeric columns. percentiles tuple[float, ...] (0.25, 0.5, 0.75) Quantiles to compute. interpolation str "nearest" Quantile interpolation method.

Returns: - DataFrame: Summary statistics table.

Examples: 

# Grouped summary statistics
df.describe(group_keys="Category", selected_columns=["Sales", "Profit"]).round(2)

docs.title: dd
docs.text:
Deduplicate rows while maintaining row order and keeping the first occurrence.

df.dd() -> DataFrame

Returns: - DataFrame: Unique rows preserving original order (equivalent to df.unique(maintain_order=True, keep='first')).

docs.title: dsort
docs.text:
Sort rows in descending order.

df.dsort(by: str | list[str] | None = None) -> DataFrame

Parameters:

Parameter Type Default Description by str, list[str], or None None Column(s) to sort by. If None, sorts by all columns.

docs.title: asort
docs.text:
Sort rows in ascending order.

df.asort(by: str | list[str] | None = None) -> DataFrame

Parameters:

Parameter Type Default Description by str, list[str], or None None Column(s) to sort by. If None, sorts by all columns.

docs.title: unstack
docs.text:
Pivot long-form data using the last two columns as the pivot key and value columns, sorted by the remaining index columns.

df.unstack() -> DataFrame

Returns: - DataFrame: Pivoted DataFrame.

docs.title: vcnt
docs.text:
Compute value frequency counts for specified column(s), sorted in descending order by count.

df.vcnt(col: str | list[str] | None = None) -> DataFrame

Parameters:

Parameter Type Default Description col str, list[str], or None None Column(s) to count. Defaults to all columns.

docs.title: ucnt
docs.text:
Compute the total distinct / unique count of rows or values.

df.ucnt(col: str | list[str] | None = None) -> int

Returns: - int: Scalar integer count of distinct values.

docs.title: round
docs.text:
Round all floating-point columns across the DataFrame.

df.round(decimal: int = 2) -> DataFrame

Parameters:

Parameter Type Default Description decimal int 2 Number of decimal places.

docs.title: cum_max
docs.text:
Calculate the cumulative maximum across all floating-point columns.

df.cum_max() -> DataFrame

docs.title: to_list
docs.text:
Extract values of a column directly into a native Python list.

df.to_list(col_name: str | None = None) -> list

Parameters:

Parameter Type Default Description col_name str or None None Target column name. Defaults to the first column.

docs.title: max
docs.text:
Extract scalar maximum value from a column.

df.max(col_name: str | None = None) -> Any

docs.title: min
docs.text:
Extract scalar minimum value from a column.

df.min(col_name: str | None = None) -> Any

docs.title: size
docs.text:
Print estimated DataFrame memory footprint and optionally return the float value.

df.size(unit: str = "mb", return_size: bool = False) -> float | None

Parameters:

Parameter Type Default Description unit str "mb" Unit: "b", "kb", "mb", or "gb". return_size bool False When True, returns the float size.

docs.title: rename
docs.text:
Enhanced column rename. Accepts either a dictionary mapping or a list of new column names matching the DataFrame's width.

df.rename(new_cols: list[str] | dict[str, str]) -> DataFrame

Examples: 

# Rename by list
df.rename(["Col_A", "Col_B", "Col_C"])

# Rename by dict (standard Polars)
df.rename({"Old": "New"})

docs.title: pplot
docs.text:
Quick plotting using Pandas' plot() interface, setting the first column as the index.

df.pplot(*args, **kwargs)

docs.title: to_polars
docs.text:
Retrieve the underlying native polars.DataFrame.

df.to_polars() -> polars.DataFrame

docs.title: to_pandas
docs.text:
Convert to a pandas.DataFrame.

df.to_pandas() -> pandas.DataFrame

docs.title: String DSL & Functions Reference
docs.text: Polynx provides an integrated Domain Specific Language (DSL) for writing concise expressions inside query(), eval(), assign(), wc(), and gb().

docs.title: Operators & Precedence
docs.text: Operator Category Operators Description Examples Arithmetic +, -, *, /, //, %, ** Standard mathematical arithmetic A ** 2 - E / 10 Comparison ==, !=, <, <=, >, >= Chained comparisons 1 <= A < 10 Membership in, not in Set membership testing A in @var & B > 10 Boolean & (AND), \| (OR), ~ (NOT), not Logical expressions (A > 1) & not B.is_null() Negation -, ~, not Unary negation -A + 5, ~flag Assignment = Column mutation in wc() Col = A * 2 Sequencing ; Separator for multiple statements A = 1; B = 2

docs.title: case_when
docs.text:
Unified conditional branching supporting both multi-condition and ternary logic.

case_when(conds, choices, default)

Parameters:

Parameter Type Description conds list[bool] or bool Condition expression(s). If a list is passed, checks sequentially. choices list[Any] or Any Values corresponding to each condition. default Any Value returned if no conditions match.

Examples: 

# Multi-condition branching
df.wc("Tier = case_when([Score >= 90, Score >= 75], ['Gold', 'Silver'], 'Bronze')")

# Single-condition branching (ternary)
df.wc("Flag = case_when(Score > 50, 'Pass', 'Fail')")

docs.title: select
docs.text:
Multi-condition branching mirroring numpy.select.

select(conds, choices, default)

Parameters:

Parameter Type Description conds list[bool] List of boolean condition expressions. choices list[Any] List of choices corresponding to each condition. default Any Default fallback value.

Examples: 

df.wc("Category = select([A == 1, A == 2], ['First', 'Second'], 'Other')")

docs.title: where
docs.text:
Single-condition branching mirroring numpy.where.

where(cond, choice, default)

Parameters:

Parameter Type Description cond bool Condition expression. choice Any Value returned when cond is true. default Any Value returned when cond is false.

Examples: 

df.wc("Status = where(A >= 10, 'High', 'Low')")

docs.title: mondf
docs.text:
Calculates the difference in calendar months between two date or datetime columns.

mondf(beg_date, end_date)

Formula: $$\text{mondf} = (\text{end_date.year} - \text{beg_date.year}) \times 12 + (\text{end_date.month} - \text{beg_date.month})$$

Examples: 

df.wc("Month_Lag = mondf(Date_Col, Date_Col.shift())")

docs.title: max_horizontal
docs.text:
Computes the row-wise maximum across multiple column expressions:

df.wc("Row_Max = max_horizontal(A, B, C)")

docs.title: min_horizontal
docs.text:
Computes the row-wise minimum across multiple column expressions:

df.wc("Row_Min = min_horizontal(A, B, C)")

docs.title: Variable Substitution (@var)
docs.text:
Prefixing an identifier with @ dynamically retrieves variables from the executing Python environment.

target_id = 42
categories = ['A', 'B']
cutoff_date = '2022-01-01'

df.query("ID == @target_id & Cat in @categories & Date > @cutoff_date")

docs.title: Supported Variable Types:
docs.text:
• Scalars: Integers, floats, strings, booleans, dates.
  • Iterables: Lists, tuples, sets.
  • Arrays & Series: NumPy arrays, Pandas Series, Polars Series.

docs.title: Identifier Escaping (Backticks)
docs.text:
Column names that contain whitespace, hyphens, or special symbols can be enclosed in backticks (`):

df.query("`Sales Volume` > 1000 & `Customer-ID` == 'C10'")

docs.title: Polars Data Types in Strings
docs.text:
Reference Polars data types directly within string expressions:

Literal in String Mapped Polars Type pl.Int8, pl.Int16, pl.Int32, pl.Int64 pl.Int8, pl.Int16, pl.Int32, pl.Int64 pl.Float32, pl.Float64 pl.Float32, pl.Float64 pl.String, pl.Utf8 pl.String, pl.Utf8 pl.Boolean pl.Boolean pl.Date, pl.Datetime, pl.Duration, pl.Time Date/time types pl.Categorical, pl.Struct pl.Categorical, pl.Struct

Example: 

df.wc("C_date = C.cast(pl.Date)")

docs.title: Expressions (Expr) Reference
docs.text:
polynx.Expr wraps polars.Expr and provides extended mathematical operations.

Standard Polars Expressions

polynx.Expr delegates all standard Polars expression methods (e.g., .alias(), .sum(), .mean(), .round(), .str, .dt, etc.).

For all standard Polars expressions, please refer to the Official Polars Expressions Reference.

docs.title: rolling_prod
docs.text:
Compute the rolling product across a moving window.

Evaluated numerically via log-transformation: $$\text{rolling_prod}(x) = \exp\left(\text{rolling_sum}(\log(x))\right)$$

expr.rolling_prod(*args, **kwargs) -> Expr

Parameters: Takes the same window parameters as polars.Expr.rolling_sum:

Parameter Type Default Description window_size str or int required The length of the window (number of rows or duration string). min_samples int 1 Minimum number of non-null observations required. weights list[float] or None None Optional sequence of weights.

Returns: - Expr: Expression computing the rolling product.

Examples: 

import polynx as plx

df = plx.DataFrame({'val': [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]})
df.select(plx.col('val').rolling_prod(window_size=2, min_samples=1))

docs.title: Windowing with .over()
docs.text:
Polynx's string expression parser supports the .over() method accepting either a single column string or a list of columns:

# Single grouping key
df.wc("group_mean = val.mean().over('category')")

# Multiple grouping keys
df.wc("multi_group_mean = val.mean().over(['region', 'category'])")

docs.title: to_polars
docs.text:
Retrieve the underlying native polars.Expr.

expr.to_polars() -> polars.Expr

docs.title: Input / Output & Merge Reference
docs.text:
Polynx re-exports all public Polars top-level functions with automatic argument unwrapping and return-value wrapping.

Standard Polars IO & Construction Functions

Polynx exports all public Polars functions directly from polynx (e.g., read_csv, read_parquet, scan_csv, scan_parquet, concat, col, lit, etc.).

For full documentation on these native IO and construction functions, please consult the Official Polars IO Reference.

docs.title: merge
docs.text:
Pandas-style join interface for DataFrame or LazyFrame with automatic column suffix handling on overlapping names.

plx.merge(
    left: DataFrame | LazyFrame,
    right: DataFrame | LazyFrame,
    on: str | list[str] | None = None,
    how: str = "inner",
    suffixes: tuple[str, str] = ("_x", "_y")
) -> DataFrame | LazyFrame

Parameters:

Parameter Type Default Description left DataFrame or LazyFrame required Left table. right DataFrame or LazyFrame required Right table. on str, list[str], or None None Join column key(s). how str "inner" Join strategy: "inner", "left", "right", or "outer". suffixes tuple[str, str] ("_x", "_y") Suffixes appended to overlapping columns not in on.

Returns: - DataFrame or LazyFrame: Joined dataset.

Examples: 

import polynx as plx

df1 = plx.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2], 'val': [10, 20]})
df2 = plx.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2], 'val': [30, 40]})

merged = plx.merge(df1, df2, on='id', suffixes=('_a', '_b'))
# Columns: ['id', 'val_a', 'val_b']

docs.title: Inherited Polars Functions
docs.text: All public Polars functions are accessible directly from the polynx namespace:

docs.title: Data Creation & IO
docs.text:
# Concat DataFrames or LazyFrames
df_all = plx.concat([df1, df2])

# Reading and Writing
df = plx.read_csv("data.csv")
df = plx.read_parquet("data.parquet")

docs.title: Expression Builders
docs.text:
# Column references and literals
plx.col("Sales")
plx.lit(100)

# Native conditional expressions
plx.when(plx.col("Sales") > 50).then(1).otherwise(0)

All functions perform deep unwrapping on inputs and wrap return types back into polynx instances.

docs.title: LazyFrame Reference
docs.text:
polynx.LazyFrame wraps polars.LazyFrame with the complete suite of Polynx string expression methods and enhanced lazy indexing.

import polynx as plx

lazy_df = plx.DataFrame(data).lazy()

Standard Polars LazyFrame Methods

polynx.LazyFrame inherits all native Polars lazy operations and optimization passes.

This page covers only the Polynx-specific lazy extensions. For standard Polars LazyFrame methods, please refer to the Official Polars LazyFrame Reference.

docs.title: Lazy Execution Model
docs.text:
All operations on a LazyFrame are deferred into a query plan and executed only when .collect() is called:

result = (
    lazy_df
    .wc("A_doubled = A * 2")
    .query("A_doubled > 10")
    .collect()
)

docs.title: Methods Inherited from DataFrame
docs.text:
The following methods are implemented for LazyFrame and operate lazily:

  • query(query_str): Filters the lazy query plan using string expressions.
  • eval(query_str, mode): Evaluates string expressions lazily.
  • assign(query_str): Appends new computed columns lazily.
  • wc(*args, **kwargs): Multi-statement column mutations lazily.
  • gb(gp_keys, expr, with_subtotal): String-powered group by aggregations lazily.
  • dd(): Deduplication maintaining order.
  • dsort(by): Descending sort.
  • asort(by): Ascending sort.
  • describe(...): Evaluates and summarizes metrics.
  • round(decimal): Rounds all float columns lazily.
  • cum_max(): Cumulative maximum lazily.
  • rename(new_cols): Rename by list or dict.
  • unstack(): Pivoting (collects to eager automatically).
  • to_list(col_name): Collects and extracts column list.
  • max(col_name) / min(col_name): Collects and returns scalar.

docs.title: Lazy Indexing Syntax
docs.text: Polynx enhances LazyFrame with bracket indexing:

docs.title: Column Selection
docs.text:
# Select single column
lazy_df['column_name']

# Select multiple columns
lazy_df[['col_a', 'col_b']]

docs.title: Expression Filtering
docs.text:
import polars as pl

# Filter rows lazily via indexing
lazy_df[pl.col('A') > 5]

docs.title: collect
docs.text:
Execute the query plan and materialize a polynx.DataFrame.

lazy_df.collect() -> polynx.DataFrame

docs.title: to_polars
docs.text:
Retrieve the underlying native polars.LazyFrame.

lazy_df.to_polars() -> polars.LazyFrame

docs.title: to_pandas
docs.text:
Collects the lazy frame and converts the result into a pandas.DataFrame.

lazy_df.to_pandas() -> pandas.DataFrame

docs.title: Series Reference
docs.text:
polynx.Series is a transparent wrapper around polars.Series providing Python sequence protocol methods (__getitem__, __len__) and data conversion utilities.

import polynx as plx

s = plx.Series("name", [1, 2, 3, 4])

Standard Polars Series Methods

polynx.Series inherits all native Polars series methods (e.g., .sum(), .mean(), .filter(), .str, .dt, etc.).

For native Polars Series methods, please refer to the Official Polars Series Reference.

docs.title: __getitem__
docs.text:
Index elements or slices directly:

s = plx.Series("A", [10, 20, 30])

s[0]   # 10
s[1]   # 20
s[-1]  # 30

docs.title: __len__
docs.text:
Retrieve the length of the series using standard Python len():

len(s)  # 3

docs.title: to_polars
docs.text:
Retrieve the underlying native polars.Series.

s.to_polars() -> polars.Series

docs.title: to_pandas
docs.text:
Convert the series to a pandas.Series.

s.to_pandas() -> pandas.Series

docs.title: Delegated Polars Methods
docs.text: All native Polars Series methods (e.g., .sum(), .mean(), .std(), .filter(), .cast(), .str, .dt) are dynamically delegated and automatically wrap results back into polynx.Series.

docs.title: User Defined Functions (UDF) Reference
docs.text: Register custom Python functions to call them directly inside Polynx string expressions.

docs.title: register_udf
docs.text:
Register a single Python function under a given identifier name.

plx.register_udf(name: str, fn: callable) -> None

Parameters:

Parameter Type Description name str Name of the function as it will be called in string expressions. fn callable Python callable.

Example: 

import polynx as plx

def add_tax(price, tax_rate=0.08):
    return price * (1 + tax_rate)

plx.register_udf("add_tax", add_tax)

df = plx.DataFrame({'price': [100.0, 200.0]})
df.wc("total = add_tax(price, 0.10)")

docs.title: register_udfs_by_names
docs.text:
Register multiple functions from a module by their names.

plx.register_udfs_by_names(module: Any, names: list[str]) -> None

Parameters:

Parameter Type Description module module object Python module containing the functions. names list[str] List of function names to register.

Example: 

import math
import polynx as plx

plx.register_udfs_by_names(math, ["sin", "cos", "log10"])

df = plx.DataFrame({'x': [1.0, 10.0, 100.0]})
df.wc("log_val = log10(x)")
